title: Oncoproteins and Tumour Markers: the RAS Switch, p53 and NMP22
summary: Follow the RAS on/off switch and the p53 brake, see how hotspot mutations jam them, why RAS-mutant colorectal cancer does not benefit from anti-EGFR antibodies, and why a positive urine NMP22 still needs cystoscopy.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 76 Hits 2–5 and Traps 3–4 (first lesson for Ch. 76). Checked against Simanshu 2017, Kastenhuber & Lowe 2017, Mattioni 2015, Zhou 2016 and Wang 2017. Discrepancies: the reviewer’s blanket “95–100% specificity” for oncoprotein assays (Hit 1) is not supported — the NMP22 point-of-care test had pooled specificity 88% (register rv-oncoprotein-spec); KRAS ~75% in colon cancer (Hit 4) vs 42% in Simanshu Table 1 (register rv-kras-colon). Not taught: NMP22 cut-offs 10/5 U/mL, ras-p21 serum ranges, p53 20-minute half-life, “mostly G12V” in pancreas, single-study marker figures (Hits 6–13).

objectives: Describe the RAS GDP/GTP switch, including the roles of GEFs and GAPs.
Explain how RAS hotspot and TP53 mutations disable growth control, and why RAS status predicts anti-EGFR benefit in colorectal cancer.
Interpret a urine NMP22 result in light of its sensitivity and specificity.

Question token: “Which result changes treatment, and which needs confirmation?”

cues.text: Two reports arrive. A patient under bladder-cancer surveillance has a positive urine NMP22 test.
A patient with metastatic colorectal cancer has a KRAS codon 12 mutation, and the team is considering cetuximab.
Which result changes treatment, and which one still needs confirmation?

scenes.title: The RAS switch and the p53 brake
scenes.altText: Schematic relay (not to scale; Simanshu 2017): growth-factor receptor (RTK) → RAS·GDP (OFF) → a GEF such as SOS exchanges GDP for GTP → RAS·GTP (ON) → recruits effectors such as RAF kinase to the membrane → growth signal. A GAP (e.g. RASA1, using its “arginine finger”) speeds GTP hydrolysis → RAS·GDP (OFF). Brake card (Kastenhuber & Lowe 2017): in normal cells p53 is kept at low levels by MDM2, a ubiquitin ligase that targets it for degradation; stress such as DNA damage stabilizes p53, which can arrest the cell cycle or trigger apoptosis.

cues.text: Growth signals from receptor tyrosine kinases pass through RAS. Resting RAS holds GDP and is switched off.
An exchange factor such as SOS swaps GDP for GTP. GTP-bound RAS is on, and recruits effectors such as RAF kinase.
A GTPase-activating protein, or GAP, pokes an arginine finger into the site and speeds GTP hydrolysis, switching RAS back off.
Meanwhile p53 is a brake. In normal cells MDM2 keeps p53 low by tagging it for degradation; DNA damage stabilizes p53, which can halt the cell cycle or trigger apoptosis.

scenes.title: Stuck accelerator, cut brake
scenes.altText: Mutation card (Simanshu 2017): most RAS mutations are at codons 12, 13 or 61. Substitutions of glycine 12/13 are thought to sterically block the GAP arginine finger; Q61 mutations destroy intrinsic and GAP-mediated hydrolysis → RAS stays GTP-bound (ON) without upstream signals. Frequency bar (Simanshu Table 1, KRAS): pancreas 91%, colon 42%, lung 33%. p53 card (Kastenhuber & Lowe 2017; Mattioni 2015): about half of all cancers carry a TP53 mutation, mostly missense in the DNA-binding domain; mutant p53 has a longer half-life than wild type and accumulates in cancer cells, which can induce circulating p53 antibodies.

cues.text: In cancer, most RAS mutations hit codons 12, 13 or 61. Changing glycine 12 or 13 is thought to block the GAP arginine finger; changing glutamine 61 wrecks hydrolysis itself.
Either way, RAS stays GTP-bound and keeps signalling without any growth factor: a stuck accelerator.
KRAS is the usual culprit: mutated in about 91 percent of pancreatic cancers, 42 percent of colon cancers and 33 percent of lung cancers in one large tabulation.
The brake fails too. About half of all cancers carry a TP53 mutation, mostly missense changes in the DNA-binding domain.
Mutant p53 lasts longer than the wild type and piles up in cancer cells, and some patients make antibodies against it.

scenes.title: What the lab result can and cannot say
scenes.altText: Predictive card (Zhou 2016 meta-analysis, first-line metastatic colorectal cancer): RAS wild-type tumours benefited from adding an anti-EGFR antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab); tumours that were KRAS exon 2 wild-type but carried other RAS mutations did not benefit. Logic token (Simanshu 2017): RAS transduces signals from receptor tyrosine kinases, so blocking EGFR upstream cannot switch off a RAS that is stuck ON. Screening card (Wang 2017 meta-analysis): NMP22 tests measure nuclear mitotic apparatus protein 1 (NUMA1) with monoclonal antibodies in URINE; ELISA and point-of-care (BladderChek) formats are FDA-approved for detection and surveillance; pooled BladderChek sensitivity 56%, specificity 88%; sensitivity only ~14% for Ta tumours; cystoscopy is the gold standard. Hook answer: KRAS-mutant → anti-EGFR not expected to help; positive NMP22 → confirm by cystoscopy.

cues.text: For metastatic colorectal cancer, a meta-analysis found that RAS wild-type tumours benefited from adding cetuximab or panitumumab, but tumours with RAS mutations did not.
The logic: RAS sits downstream of the receptor. Blocking EGFR cannot switch off a RAS that is already stuck on. So test the whole RAS family, not just KRAS exon 2.
NMP22 is a urine test. It measures nuclear mitotic apparatus protein with monoclonal antibodies, in laboratory ELISA and point-of-care formats.
In a meta-analysis the point-of-care test was 56 percent sensitive and 88 percent specific, and missed most small Ta tumours. Cystoscopy remains the gold standard.
So: the KRAS mutation changes treatment, because cetuximab is not expected to help. The positive NMP22 needs cystoscopy.

props.label: EGFR → RAS: block upstream ≠ switch off
Hook: KRAS-mutant → no anti-EGFR · NMP22+ → cystoscopy

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “NMP22 is a serum test” (✓ urine; ELISA or point-of-care); “Anti-EGFR antibodies work whatever the RAS status” (✓ RAS-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer shows no benefit — RAS is downstream); “A positive tumour marker confirms cancer” (✓ NMP22 point-of-care specificity was 88% in a meta-analysis — confirm by cystoscopy).

cues.text: Trap one: NMP22 is a serum test. No: it is measured in urine, by ELISA or a point-of-care device.
Trap two: anti-EGFR antibodies work whatever the RAS status. No: RAS-mutant colorectal cancers did not benefit, because RAS sits downstream of the receptor.
Trap three: a positive tumour marker confirms cancer. No: the NMP22 point-of-care test was 88 percent specific in a meta-analysis; positives need cystoscopy.

scenes.title: Stuck accelerator, cut brake
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “RAS is the accelerator stuck down (GAP can’t lift it); p53 is the brake line cut. Block the pedal’s cable (EGFR) and a stuck accelerator still races.” Tokens: GEF = ON · GAP = OFF · G12/G13/Q61 · TP53 ~½ of cancers. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: RAS is an accelerator stuck down, because GAP can no longer lift it. p53 is a cut brake line. Cut the cable to the pedal, EGFR, and a stuck accelerator still races.

Where it breaks: some RAS mutations work by releasing GDP faster rather than blocking GAP; some mutant p53 proteins gain new functions such as promoting invasion, not just losing the brake; and a marker result is not a diagnosis.

props.title: Where it breaks

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “RAS: GEF on · GAP off · G12/G13/Q61 → stuck ON → no anti-EGFR benefit in mCRC”, “TP53 mutated in ~½ of cancers · NMP22 = urine, spec 88% → cystoscopy”.

cues.text: Hotspot RAS mutations lock RAS in its GTP-bound on state, so blocking EGFR upstream does not help RAS-mutant colorectal cancer, while screening markers such as urine NMP22 still need confirmation by cystoscopy.

props.label: RAS: GEF on · GAP off · G12/G13/Q61 stuck ON → no anti-EGFR benefit
TP53 ≈ ½ of cancers · NMP22 = urine, spec 88% → cystoscopy

explanation.what: Plain language: RAS is an on/off switch for growth signals and p53 is a brake; cancers often jam the switch on and cut the brake, and some of these changes can be measured. Scientific terms: oncoprotein, tumour suppressor, RAS·GDP/RAS·GTP, guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, e.g. SOS), GTPase-activating protein (GAP), codons 12/13/61, TP53, MDM2, anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody, NMP22 (NUMA1).
explanation.why: Hotspot RAS mutations stop GAP-driven or intrinsic GTP hydrolysis, so RAS stays on without upstream signals and blocking EGFR above it has no effect. Mutant p53 escapes normal turnover, accumulates and can provoke antibodies.
explanation.measure: Tumour RAS genotyping (KRAS and NRAS) before anti-EGFR therapy in metastatic colorectal cancer. Urine NMP22 by ELISA or point-of-care device (pooled BladderChek sensitivity 56%, specificity 88%; Wang 2017). Serum p53 antibodies are more frequent in cancer than in controls but have low sensitivity (Mattioni 2015).
explanation.differs: RAS (oncogene: activating mutation, switch stuck ON) vs TP53 (tumour suppressor: brake lost); predictive marker (RAS → therapy choice) vs screening/surveillance marker (NMP22 → needs cystoscopy).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: GEF vs GAP roles, why a KRAS-mutant colorectal cancer will not respond to cetuximab, that NMP22 is a urine test, and that a positive tumour marker requires confirmation.

questions.stem: Which protein switches RAS OFF by accelerating hydrolysis of its bound GTP?

options.rationale: Correct. GAPs (e.g. RASA1) speed GTP hydrolysis, returning RAS to the GDP-bound off state.

options.text: A guanine nucleotide exchange factor such as SOS
options.rationale: Incorrect. GEFs swap GDP for GTP and turn RAS on.
Incorrect. MDM2 is a ubiquitin ligase that keeps p53 levels low.
Incorrect. RAF is an effector recruited by GTP-bound RAS; it carries the signal on.

questions.stem: A metastatic colorectal cancer is KRAS exon 2 wild-type but carries an NRAS codon 61 mutation. What is expected if an anti-EGFR antibody is added to chemotherapy?

options.text: No meaningful benefit, because the RAS mutation keeps signalling on downstream of EGFR
options.rationale: Correct. In the Zhou 2016 meta-analysis, tumours with other RAS mutations did not benefit; RAS sits downstream of the receptor.

options.text: Full benefit, because KRAS exon 2 is wild-type
options.rationale: Incorrect. Testing only KRAS exon 2 misses other RAS mutations that also predict no benefit.

options.text: Benefit, because NRAS mutations make EGFR overactive
options.rationale: Incorrect. The mutation is downstream of EGFR; blocking the receptor cannot switch it off.

options.text: It cannot be predicted from RAS status
options.rationale: Incorrect. RAS status is the established predictor of anti-EGFR benefit in this setting.

questions.stem: A patient under bladder-cancer surveillance has a positive urine NMP22 point-of-care test. What is the best next step?

options.text: Cystoscopy, because NMP22 is not specific enough to confirm cancer
options.rationale: Correct. Pooled specificity was 88% and sensitivity 56%; cystoscopy is the gold standard.
Incorrect. NMP22 is a urine test.
Incorrect. A marker result is not a diagnosis; confirm first.

options.text: Use the result to identify which organ the tumour arose in
options.rationale: Incorrect. The question is whether bladder cancer has recurred; that needs cystoscopy.

claims.text: RAS GDP/GTP cycle, GEF/GAP roles, hotspot mechanisms, KRAS frequencies.
TP53 mutated in about half of cancers; MDM2 regulation; mutant accumulation and antibodies.
RAS-mutant mCRC does not benefit from anti-EGFR antibodies.
NMP22 is a urine NUMA1 immunoassay; pooled BladderChek sensitivity 56%, specificity 88%; cystoscopy gold standard.

NMP22 cut-offs (10 and 5 U/mL); serum ras-p21 ranges; wild-type p53 20-minute half-life; anti-p53 15% vs 1%; “mostly G12V” in pancreas; oncoprotein specificity 95–100%; Hits 6–13 single-study figures.
claims.note: Not taught as facts; no open source read for these figures.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer gives oncoprotein assays a blanket 95–100% specificity, so that a positive “strongly implies malignancy”. Specificity is marker- and setting-specific: the NMP22 BladderChek test, listed in the same chapter, had pooled specificity 88% (Wang 2017), and positives require cystoscopy.
The reviewer states KRAS mutations in “~75% of colon cancers”; Simanshu 2017 Table 1 gives 42% for colon. Frequencies vary by study, but ~75% is well above this tabulation.
